tagline: River towns and Dakota historic sites line a glacial valley
intro: The Minnesota River Valley Scenic Byway follows a series of roads from Browns Valley to Belle Plaine, passing farmland, woods and river towns. FHWA lists it as a National Scenic Byway and emphasizes the combination of history, agriculture and culture along the river. Its description points to hardwood forests, rock outcrops and surviving prairie grasses. FHWA suggests three to seven days for visiting the byway, depending on the number of stops and time spent at each.

The valley’s shape predates these roads: Glacial River Warren cut a channel up to five miles wide and 250 feet deep at the end of the last ice age. The byway connects sites associated with Dakota history and the U.S.-Dakota War of 1862. At the Lower Sioux Agency, the federal government administered the reservation established for the Mdewakanton and Wahpekute bands following the 1851 Treaty of Mendota.

From Browns Valley, the journey follows the river from its source at Big Stone Lake toward Belle Plaine. Lac qui Parle Mission and the Lower Sioux Agency are historical stops along the route. New Ulm’s German heritage is reflected in its festivals. The river runs southeast to Mankato before turning northeast; the byway continues toward Belle Plaine through a landscape of farms and river communities.

moments.title: Lac qui Parle Mission
moments.text: The mission building at Lac qui Parle is a 1942 Works Progress Administration reconstruction. The original mission began in 1835 after fur trader Joseph Renville invited missionaries to the area. Work here included the first Dakota-language dictionary and the first translation of part of the Bible into Dakota. Relations between the mission and Dakota people worsened after Renville’s death, and the missionaries left for the Upper Sioux Agency in 1854. Renville’s nearby fortified home and trading post had been a stopping place for traders on the Red River Trails. The reconstructed mission is managed by the Chippewa County Historical Society with the Minnesota Historical Society.

moments.title: Lower Sioux Agency
moments.text: An 1861 stone warehouse is the only surviving structure of the Lower Sioux Agency. The United States government established the agency in 1853 to administer the Lower Sioux reservation. On August 15, 1862, agent Thomas J. Galbraith refused to distribute food without payment from treaty annuities that had been delayed. Three days later, the first organized battle of the U.S.-Dakota War took place here. The Lower Sioux Community now manages the historic site with the Minnesota Historical Society; in 2021 the society transferred ownership of half the site to the community.
moments.notice: Interpretive signs mark lost agency features, including the Redwood Ferry crossing.

moments.title: Hermann Heights Monument
moments.text: Hermann’s raised sword and eastward gaze are part of a monument to German heritage above New Ulm. The figure depicts Arminius, remembered for the German victory over Roman forces at the Battle of the Teutoburg Forest. The Sons of Hermann fraternal order paid for the monument under the leadership of Julius Berndt, who designed its setting. The statue arrived in 1890 and was dedicated in 1897. Its copper skin is molded over iron, and the supporting structure rests on a Kasota stone base. Nearby, St. Paul atop the Cathedral of the Holy Trinity also faces east, but his sword points down.
